original_value:
Emoji are widely used in computer-mediated communication to express concepts and emotions. Skin tone modifiers were added in 2015 with the hope of better representing user diversity, and, indeed, recent work has shown that these modifiers are especially popular among darker-skinned users, who are a minority on Twitter. Previous work also showed that the vast majority of tone-modified emoji have a tone similar to the user’s own skin tone, suggesting that self-representation is a major factor in tone use. In this article, we first show that the basic finding (users mainly choose a tone that is similar to their own skin tone) generalizes to different sub-populations of users, including users from majority-Black regions. We then extend the analysis of tone use to quantify and examine cases where users
            modulate
            their tones—that is, for a particular emoji, they choose either to use a different tone than their usual one or no tone at all (after having previously used one). We show that even though these uses constitute only a small proportion of emoji usage, many instances are readily classifiable as ways of representing
            other
            people. The evidence we present is therefore crucial in working toward a broader understanding of the connection between emoji and identity expression online. We also offer explanations for why the darkest emoji skin tones are not used, by examining aspects of their design, which make them less suited to self-representational usage. This highlights the need for careful consideration of both design and human diversity when creating emoji. Moreover, despite early fears in the media, we find little evidence of negative usage, even when tones are used in a non-self-representational manner. In sum, our findings lend even more support to the highly positive role that emoji and skin tone modifiers play in identity and expression in computer-mediated communication.

result.paraphrase: Emoji are commonly used in computer-mediated communication to convey emotions and ideas. Skin tone modifiers, introduced in 2015 to better reflect user diversity, have been shown in recent work to be especially popular among darker-skinned users, who are a minority on Twitter. Prior studies also found that most tone-modified emoji match the user’s own skin tone, indicating that self-representation is a key driver of tone choice. In this article, we first demonstrate that this core pattern—users mainly selecting a tone similar to their own skin tone—holds across different user sub-populations, including those from majority-Black regions. We then expand the study of tone use to measure and analyze cases in which users modulate their tones, meaning that for a given emoji they either pick a tone different from their usual one or use no tone at all after previously using one. We show that although these cases make up only a small share of emoji use, many of them can be readily interpreted as representing other people. The evidence we present is therefore essential to building a broader understanding of how emoji and identity expression are linked online. We also explain why the darkest emoji skin tones are seldom used by examining design aspects that make them less suitable for self-representational use. This underscores the importance of considering both design and human diversity when creating emoji. Moreover, despite early media fears, we find little evidence of negative usage, even when tones are used in a non-self-representational way. Overall, our findings further support the strongly positive role that emoji and skin tone modifiers play in identity and expression in computer-mediated communication.
